title: Leveling the Playing Field -- Ch. 10: Borderless Justice
keywords: the only Latin American nation in Asia
Appellate Body of the World Trade Organization
Economic, Social and Cultural Rights Covenant
patents, trademarks and intellectual property rights
primary_topics: Chapter 10 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' -- CJP's address on the 'Globalization of Justice' to the First Global Biotechnology Forum in Concepcion, Chile, arguing that because human rights, trade, health, science and information are now worldwide, 'so must law and justice be globalized.'

The dilution of the territorial doctrine: laws and judgments were traditionally binding only within national borders, but international tribunals, telecommunications, migration, technology and 'the scientific realities of our ever-shrinking world' have modified that absoluteness and created demand for the universalization of justice.

Two borderless viruses as proof -- the SARS epidemic, which showed that 'scientific and medical issues are, at heart, questions about human rights and social policy,' and the 'ILoveYou' computer virus, whose Filipino creator escaped prosecution because no Philippine law then punished computer crimes and the 'double criminality' clause blocked extradition.

The coming docket of the bio-age -- genetic engineering, embryo ownership, cloning, cryogenics, heirship, GMO labeling, DNA identification, genetic information and patents -- which should be 'resolved uniformly by various national tribunals in order to avoid the evils of forum shopping.'

The closing qualification that 'globalization is not necessarily antagonistic to nationalism,' requiring only that sovereignty rooted in artificial borders be deemphasized, since national identity is never homogeneous -- as the Filipino diaspora shows.
sub_topics: He opens with the distance travelled -- 'from east to west and from north to south' -- to address a forum jointly organized by UNIDO and the Government of Chile, and claims instant identification with his hosts.

He explains the affinity: the Philippines is often called 'the only Latin American nation in Asia,' the only Christian nation in its part of the globe and the only one colonized by both Spain and the United States, sharing the Latin American passion for life, music, dance and the arts.

He connects that affinity to FEALAC or FOCALE, whose 32 countries had met in Manila on January 28-31, 2004, only the second such gathering of foreign ministers after Santiago in March 2000, and notes he is the only Filipino jurist invited to speak.

He states the traditional postulate that laws and judicial decisions are territorial, flowing from the centuries-old view that sovereignty is absolute only within a state's boundary, and notes the emerging international tribunals -- the ICJ, the WTO Appellate Body and the International Criminal Court.

He argues that even within national systems judges face controversies that transcend borders, as trade, banking, intellectual property, immigration, human rights, human dignity and criminal law enforcement build 'a burgeoning literature on the globalization of justice.'

He distinguishes globalization from trade alone -- beyond the street debates over McDonald's and Starbucks -- defining it as an interconnected process of institutional, demographic and cultural connection and a consciousness that some issues can no longer be addressed nationally.

He contends that human rights have been propelled by globalization more than and ahead of trade, having helped bring down the Soviet empire, transformed South America and strengthened the United Nations.

He cites Professor Hans Köchler's 'Global Justice or Global Revenge' for the view that national sovereignty must be redefined against the universal validity of human rights, which as norms of jus cogens 'transcend the confines of traditional state-centered international law.'

He observes that the wars on terror in Afghanistan and Iraq have metamorphosed the concept of a just war from an armed response to invasion into 'seek and destroy' operations against terrorists wherever found, further eroding national sovereignty.

SARS: the virus 'respected no territorial boundaries,' and state responses were determined not by science alone but by law and politics; countries that suppressed reporting could not respond promptly, while open societies could not hide the reports yet faced court challenges to quarantine, sealing off neighborhoods and slaughtering animal carriers.

The epidemic demonstrated the need for global cooperation -- monitoring at points of origin, transit and destination -- and made the WHO, whose alerts 'virtually decided the fates of economies and industries,' the only credible authority when every state belittled its own infection.

The lesson he draws is that the universal 'right to health,' protected under the Economic, Social and Cultural Rights Covenant and the Civil and Political Rights Covenant, 'could actually be secured by citizens through their local courts,' with AIDS, mad cow disease and avian flu posing similar global questions.

The cyber parallel: the 'ILoveYou' virus crippled computer systems worldwide in 2000 and was traced to a student in a Philippine computer school, but he could not be prosecuted because no Philippine law then punished computer crimes, and the 'double criminality' clause of the Philippine-US Extradition Treaty stumped American authorities -- with 'MyDoom' then alarming the world's websites.

He lists the science questions needing juridical answers: disputes from genetic engineering of humans, animals and plants; embryo ownership, fertility, abortion, reproductive rights, paternity and heirship; access to reproductive technology and the question of human cloning; cryogenics; access to drugs and treatments; and GMO regulation, with the European Union recognizing the consumer's right to information and mandating labeling.

He notes DNA testing's rise as a judicial tool, citing Time magazine that nearly 80 convicts under final judgment in the United States were exonerated by DNA evidence, and the new controversies over genetic information, body parts, tissues and genetic testing, along with a surge in patent and trademark infringement questions.

He closes by congratulating the sponsors for anticipating the judicial issues of the biosciences and the participants for combining science and law, so they may return home 'better prepared to meet the challenges of the bio-age.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 10 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' collects CJP's address on the 'Globalization of Justice' to the First Global Biotechnology Forum in Concepcion, Chile, organized by UNIDO and the Chilean government. He opened by claiming affinity with his hosts, since the Philippines is often called the only Latin American nation in Asia, the only Christian nation in its part of the globe and the only one colonized by both Spain and the United States, and linked that affinity to the FEALAC or FOCALE ministers' meeting held in Manila that January. He then stated the traditional postulate that laws and judicial decisions are territorial, flowing from the view that sovereignty is absolute only within a state's boundary, and argued that international tribunals, telecommunications, migration, technology and an ever-shrinking world had modified that absoluteness. Globalization, he said, was more than trade: it was an interconnected process of institutional, demographic and cultural connection, and human rights had been propelled by it ahead of trade, citing Hans Köchler for the view that sovereignty must be redefined against human rights as norms of jus cogens, while the wars on terror had transformed the concept of just war. He offered two borderless viruses as proof. SARS respected no boundaries, showed that medical questions were at heart questions of human rights and social policy, exposed both the suppression of reporting in closed systems and the legal barriers to quarantine in open ones, and made the WHO the only credible authority, teaching that the right to health could be secured through local courts. The 'ILoveYou' virus, created by a Philippine student, crippled systems worldwide yet left its author unpunished, since no Philippine law then covered computer crimes and the double criminality clause blocked extradition. He surveyed the coming bio-age docket -- genetic engineering, embryo disposition, cloning, cryogenics, GMO labeling, DNA identification and patents -- urging uniform national decisions to avoid forum shopping, and closed that globalization is not necessarily antagonistic to nationalism.
